“The men in Frankfurt wanted to found a Reich whose existence would have amounted to a general European revolution, and they calculated the future on the basis of the illusions in which the revolutionary excitement of the moment was living.”
B. Bauer, Der Untergang des Frankfurter Parlaments. Geschichte der deutschen constituirenden Nationalversammlung, Berlin 1849, p. 94.
Schmitt also uses this sentence to open the essay on Donoso mentioned below.
Donoso essay — [C. Schmitt], “Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation,” in Die neue Ordnung 3, 1949, no. 1, pp. 1–15, published without the author’s name.

The essay originated in a lecture delivered in Spanish in Madrid on 31 May 1944 and was anonymously published in 1949 under the title “Donoso Cortés y las revoluciones de 1848,” in Revista de la Faculdad de derecho y ciencias sociales de la Universidad de Buones Aires 4, 1949, no. 17, pp. 13–26. In 1950 it appeared as chapter 4 of the book published under the same title.

the refuge offered by the Dominicans — During these years Schmitt received support at the Dominican monastery of Walberberg, especially from its prior, Father Eberhard Welty, who edited the journal Die neue Ordnung.
P.[asserin] d’Entrèves — Alessandro Passerin d’Entrèves (1902–1985), Italian philosopher of law.
“Above my cap only the stars” — See Goethe, West-östlicher Divan, in Goethes Werke, ed. Erich Trunz, Hamburg edition, vol. 2, p. 9:
“Let me count for something only in my saddle! Remain in your huts and in your tents! And I ride happily into the distance, Above my cap only the stars.”

I wish to be thought, I who am wholly thought — From the New Testament apocrypha, Acts of John 95. See Die Apokryphen Schriften zum Neuen Testament, trans. and annotated by Wilhelm Michaelis, Bremen 1956, p. 251, where the wording is: “I wish to be thought, for I am thought through and through.”
“The Man in the Cell” — Refers to Nicolaus Sombart, “Der Mann in der Zelle,” in Nordseezeitung (Bremen), 2 March 1949.
On 10 March 1949 Schmitt wrote to Sombart:

“‘The Man in the Cell’ has rekindled my old affection for you. There are moments in it that reveal your own distinctive genius. For me, one example is the passage on Goethe’s line ‘above my cap only the stars.’ Other parts seem too psychological to me, too much like topical conversation and reflections that lie too close at hand. Every paragraph, indeed every sentence, keeps me occupied.”

Hans Zehrer — (1899–1966), journalist and leading figure of the Tat circle; editor-in-chief of the Sonntagsblatt from 1948 to 1953 and of Die Welt from 1953 to 1966. He had known Carl Schmitt since 1931.

letter from Gottfried Benn — G. Benn, “Ein Berliner Brief,” in Merkur 3, 1949, pp. 203–206. This letter, written in July 1948 to the editor of Merkur, marked the beginning of Benn’s postwar comeback. See G. Benn, Gesammelte Werke in vier Bänden, ed. D. Wellershoff, vol. 4, 3rd ed., Wiesbaden 1977, pp. 280–285.

the German judges on trial in Luxembourg — Trials were held in Luxembourg in 1948–1949 against German judges who had served on special and emergency courts during the war. Most of the charges proved impossible to sustain. See Matthias Herbers, Organisationen im Krieg (Beiträge zur Rechtsgeschichte des 20. Jahrhunderts, 71), Tübingen 2012, pp. 24 ff.
Donoso essay, anonymous — See the note above on p. 168.

the depressing discussion about democracy and elites — At 9:15 p.m. on 15 March 1949, Radio Frankfurt’s evening program broadcast a debate entitled “Masse und Elite” [“Mass and Elite”]. The participants were Heinrich Gremmels (“son of a secondary-school teacher”), Friedrich Minssen, Gerhard Nebel (“former secondary-school teacher”), and Nicolaus Sombart (“son of a sociologist”). See Schmittiana VII, 2001, p. 92, note 6, and BW Sombart, p. 20.
remark by Danzenbrinck — Franz Danzenbrinck (1899–1960), lawyer and local politician. Schmitt wished he had made the remark himself; see BW Mohler, p. 52.

“The trend from unanimity to majority” — Schmitt is referring to Paul Guggenheim, Lehrbuch des Völkerrechts. Unter Berücks. d. internat. u. schweizer. Praxis, installments 1–3, Basel 1947–1948. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, nos. 22936–22938.
In note 141, the sentence is sourced as follows: Cromwell A. Riches, Majority Rule in International Organization. A Study of the Trend from Unanimity to Majority Decision, Baltimore 1940.

friend Barth — Karl Barth (1886–1968), Swiss Reformed theologian who understood God as the “wholly Other” and whose thinking therefore stood in a tense relationship with Carl Schmitt’s. See Mathias Eichhorn, Es wird regiert! Der Staat im Denken Karl Barths und Carl Schmitts in den Jahren 1919 bis 1938 (Beiträge zur politischen Wissenschaft, 78), Berlin 1994. See also above, pp. 277–278.
Rapinam arbitrantes justitiam — “Taking robbery for justice.”

The Vulgate text of Philippians 2:6 reads: qui cum in forma Dei esset non rapinam arbitratus est esse se aequalem Deo. Luther translates: “He, who was in divine form, did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God.”

The knowing spirit, the spirit that knows itself … — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: G. W. F. Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes (= Sämtliche Werke. Krit. Gesamtausgabe der Werke Hegels in zwölf Bänden, ed. and introduced by Otto Weiß), Leipzig 1909. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24638.

occultus propter metum Judaeorum — Vulgate, John 19:38: post haec autem rogavit Pilatum Ioseph ab Arimathia eo quod esset discipulus Iesu occultus autem propter metum Iudaeorum ut tolleret corpus Iesu.
Luther: “After this, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, though secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate to allow him to take down the body of Jesus.”
**Pascual Jordan, Physik im Fortschritt*** — Correctly: Pascual Jordan, *Physik im Vordringen (Die Wissenschaft, 99), Braunschweig 1949. Schmitt received a copy from the author with a dedication.

Heinrich Triepel’s “Vom Stil im Recht” — Correctly: Heinrich Triepel, Vom Stil des Rechts. Beiträge zu einer Ästhetik des Rechts, Heidelberg 1947. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 22862.

Tigges, Nebel — Hubert Tigges (1895–1971), travel entrepreneur and publisher at Marée-Verlag in Wuppertal, which published Gerhard Nebel’s books, including Ernst Jünger und das Schicksal des Menschen, 1948 (copy in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 22281), and Ernst Jünger. Abenteuer des Geistes, 1949 (RW 265, no. 22279).
“means of complete comprehension …” — P. Jordan, Physik im Vordringen, cited above, p. 55.

**the filiaque instead of the filioque*** — The statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father “and from the Son” (filioque*) refers to the central dogmatic issue over which the Eastern and Western Churches split in the sixth century.
Schmitt may also have been influenced here by the fact that, besides both being fathers of daughters, Fleig’s wife was said to resemble Duška Schmitt very closely; see BW Mohler, p. 67.
ἀναδυομένη — “she who rises from the sea,” an epithet of the goddess Aphrodite.

ὁμοούσιος or ὁμοιούσιος — “of the same being” or “of similar being.” This was the central dogmatic controversy in the early Church between the Arians, who held that the Son of God was merely similar to the Father, and the Nicenes, who insisted that Father and Son were of the same substance. The Nicene position ultimately prevailed and remains part of the Creed used by Christian churches today.
Lietzmann — Hans Lietzmann, Geschichte der alten Kirche, vol. 1: Die Anfänge, Berlin and elsewhere, 1932.

Finance, mot d’esclave — “This word ‘finance’ is the language of a slave; it is unknown in the City.” J. J. Rousseau, Du contrat social, Amsterdam 1762, p. 133. Schmitt had already quoted this in Carl Schmitt, Die geistesgeschichtliche Lage des heutigen Parlamentarismus, 8th ed., Berlin 1996, first published Munich/Leipzig 1923, pp. 19–20.

He EK-sists, he has his being in the There; his being is Da-sein — “Man is not the lord of beings. Man is the shepherd of Being. […] Yet this is at the same time a humanism in which what is at stake is not man, but the historical essence of man in its origin from the truth of Being. But does not man’s ek-sistence itself then stand or fall in this game? It does.”
Martin Heidegger, Brief über den Humanismus, in Heidegger, Gesamtausgabe, vol. 9, Frankfurt am Main 1976, pp. 342–343; first published in 1949.
poor, good, decent Weizsäcker — Ernst von Weizsäcker was sentenced in Nuremberg to five years in prison on 14 April 1949; see the note above on p. 135.
obéissance préalable — See the note above on p. 25.
Ordo dispensatorius — an order concerning the management of the household; this refers to Gregory the Great. See the following note.
quibusdam praelati videamur … — “to those over whom we appear to have been placed. The secret dispensation puts some below others.”

Schmitt quotes Gregory the Great from Ernst Troeltsch, Die Soziallehren der christlichen Kirchen und Gruppen (= Gesammelte Schriften, 1), Tübingen 1912, p. 166. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 22087.

Kant’s great note — “The ruler of the people—the legislator—cannot at the same time be the governor, because the governor stands under the law and is therefore bound by it, hence by someone else, the sovereign. The sovereign can also take the governor’s power away, remove him, or reform his administration, but cannot punish him […], because that would once again be an act of executive power, whose highest authority is precisely the power to compel in accordance with the law. Yet this executive power would itself then be subject to coercion, which is a contradiction.”
Immanuel Kant, Metaphysik der Sitten, in Kant, Werke in zehn Bänden, ed. Wilhelm Weischedel, Darmstadt 1975, vol. 7, p. 436.
crimen immortale, inexpiabile — In Kant’s translation: a “crime that remains forever and can never be wiped away”; cited above, p. 441.
a deo excitatus — See the note above on p. 5.
blind Samson — Biblical figure from the Book of Judges, chapters 14–16.
ἦθος — “ethos”: 1. one’s usual dwelling place; 2. habit, custom, or established practice; 3. character, way of thinking, disposition. From W. Pape, Griechisch-deutsches Handwörterbuch.

“There can be no heroes in the state …” — Not a literal quotation. Schmitt is referring to §§ 93 and 218 of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right; see C. Schmitt, Hamlet oder Hekuba, 2nd ed., Stuttgart 1993, p. 65.
fame praesenti, fame futura famelicus, taedio futuro taediatus — “hungry from present hunger,” “made hungry by future hunger,” “made disgusted by future disgust.”
The phrase fame futura famelicus refers to Thomas Hobbes, De homine, X.4; see BW Mohler, p. 346.

Tocqueville says — Schmitt is referring to Alexis de Tocqueville, Mélanges, fragments historiques et notes sur l’Ancien Régime, la Révolution et l’Empire. Voyages — Pensées entièrement inédits, Paris 1865.
Arnold Toynbee’s essay of April 1949 — A. Toynbee, “Russian Catfish and Western Herring,” in the New York Herald Tribune, 12 April 1949.

docui, sed frustra — “I taught, but in vain.” The sentence from Hobbes’s Leviathan, often quoted by Schmitt—for example at the end of his own Leviathan book—is actually written by Hobbes in the present tense: doceo, sed frustra, “I teach, but in vain.” Thomas Hobbes, Opera philosophica, ed. G. Molesworth, vol. 3, London 1841, p. 213.
I am reading Emery Reves — E. Reves, Die Anatomie des Friedens, translated from the American edition by Friedrich Fischer, Zurich/Vienna/New York 1947; first published in New York in 1945.
Paci non pactis sed poenis (legibus = legibus poenalibus) providendum — “Peace and security must therefore be secured not through agreements but through punishments.” Hobbes, M/B, p. 133.
Who is so stupid that he cannot see the fraud? And who so bold that he will say he sees it? — Shakespeare, King Richard III, Act III, Scene 6.

Bachofen turns Epimetheus into a dull hylic man — See Johann Jacob Bachofen, Der Mythus von Orient und Occident. Eine Metaphysik der Alten Welt, with an introduction by Alfred Baeumler, ed. Manfred Schroeter, Munich 1926, pp. 318–319. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24846.
Carl Spitteler — (1845–1924), Swiss poet and author of the epic Prometheus und Epimetheus.

“the need of the person who acts to appear” — Max Kommerell, Schiller als Gestalter des handelnden Menschen. Gedenkrede gehalten in der Universität Bonn am 9. November 1934 (Wissenschaft und Gegenwart, 6), Frankfurt am Main 1934, p. 20. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 27868.

“like a prostitute in a tavern” — “The German people hailed and worshipped their National Assembly of 1848 like a goddess of freedom, only to let it perish one year later ‘like a prostitute in a tavern’—such was the judgment of the Spanish diplomat Donoso Cortés in his speech on the general situation in Europe on 30 January 1850.”
Veit Valentin, Geschichte der deutschen Revolution von 1848–49, Berlin 1930–1931, vol. 2, p. 1.
“Yet he is not the son of my heart …” — F. Schiller, Demetrius, Act II, Scene 1. Correctly: “Yet even if he were …”
the coinage “discriminating concept of war” — C. Schmitt, Die Wendung zum diskriminierenden Kriegsbegriff, Munich/Leipzig 1938; annotated reprint in FoP, pp. 518–597.
Kommerell’s lecture — See Max Kommerell, Schiller als Gestalter des handelnden Menschen. Gedenkrede gehalten in der Universität Bonn am 9. November 1934, Frankfurt am Main 1934, pp. 15–16.
**Erich Voegelin’s Rassenidee*** — Erich Voegelin, *Die Rassenidee in der Geistesgeschichte von Ray bis Carus, Berlin 1933. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 25790.
Churchill’s speech — In a speech to the House of Commons on 21 April 1944, Churchill said: “In a world of confusion and ruin the old flag flies.”
Schmitt was in Portugal from 13 to 23 May 1944, so he cannot have heard the speech there.

“Et le vent furibond de la concupiscence …” — From Charles Baudelaire’s poem “Femmes damnées” in the collection L’Épaves. In Baudelaire, Sämtliche Werke/Briefe, ed. Friedhelm Kemp and Claude Pichois, vol. 4, Munich/Vienna 1975, pp. 14 ff.
